requirement: Habeas MUST identify a Rust item by the pair of its `rust_file`, following the path rules in {cite}`requirements.ci.schema`, and a `rust_item` selector derived from a `syn` parse of that file. The selector MUST describe syntactic ancestry within the file and MUST NOT resolve Rust modules across files or use line numbers as identity. Named items MUST use kind-and-name segments such as `fn[run]` and `struct[Packet]`. Impl segments MUST distinguish inherent from trait impls using their syntactic self type and optional trait path. Otherwise identical selectors MUST have deterministic source-order disambiguators. A `use` declaration MUST have a positional selector `use#N`, where N is its one-based position among sibling `use` declarations; its import target MUST NOT form part of the selector. Other items without a suitable name MUST have a kind and positional disambiguator. Selector spelling MUST be documented and reversible when names or types contain delimiter characters.
rationale:
**Judgment: true.** `src/rust_items.rs` implements each obligation of `requirements.references.rust_item_selectors`, and one unit test covers the main design cases. A few secondary cases have no test; they are listed at the end and do not change the verdict.

**Implementation**
- **Parse and scope.**
  - `parse_items` (src/rust_items.rs) calls `syn::parse_file`, then walks the tree with `ItemCollector`. The collector's `visit_item`, `visit_impl_item`, `visit_trait_item` and `visit_foreign_item` maintain a `parents` stack.
  - The selector is the parent's selector joined with `/` to the item's own segment. It records only syntactic ancestry within the one file. It does no module resolution, so `mod external;` is just `mod[external]`.
  - Line numbers are not part of identity. They are stored separately in `RustItem`.
- **Named items.** `named()` produces `fn[run]`, `struct[Packet]`, `mod[x]`, `trait[x]`, `const[x]`, `type[x]` and so on. `extern "C"` blocks become `extern[C]`, and `ForeignItem::Fn` gives `extern[C]/fn[puts]`.
- **Impl segments.** An inherent impl is `impl[SelfType]`. A trait impl is `impl[SelfType/Trait]`. Both are built from the source text of `self_ty` and the trait path.
- **Duplicates.** Items are grouped by `(parent, base)` and sorted by `byte_start`. Any group with more than one member gets `#1`, `#2`, … in source order. This applies at every nesting level, including duplicate impl blocks.
- **`use` and unnamed items.**
  - `use` has the base `use` with `ordinal_always = true`, so it is always `use#N`. The import target is never part of the selector.
  - The same `ordinal_always` mechanism gives the positional form `item#N` or `macro#N` to other unnamed items (verbatim items, macro invocations).
- **Escaping.** `escape_segment` percent-encodes `%`, `[`, `]`, `/`, `#` and whitespace as UTF-8 bytes. Encoding `%` itself keeps the mapping injective, so the spelling is reversible.
- **Lookup and documentation.**
  - `src/inputs.rs` (around lines 155–170) resolves a `rust_file` and `rust_item` pair by exact selector match. It rejects an unknown selector and an ambiguous one.
  - The selector syntax, examples, duplicate rule, `use#N` and percent-encoding are documented in the "References" section of `md/reference.md`.

**Tests**
- `mod[tests]/fn[selectors_name_syntactic_ancestry_and_duplicates]` parses a fixture and asserts these selectors:
  - `use#1` and `use#2`;
  - `mod[local]/fn[run]` and `mod[external]`;
  - `struct[Thing]`;
  - `impl[Thing]/fn[run]` and `impl[Thing/Trait]/fn[run]`;
  - `trait[Trait]/fn[read]`;
  - `extern[C]/fn[puts]`;
  - `fn[outer]/fn[inner]`;
  - `fn[repeated]#1` and `fn[repeated]#2` for `#[cfg]`-guarded siblings;
  - `impl[%5Bu8;%204%5D]/fn[edge]`, which exercises escaping of brackets and whitespace in an impl self type.
- The test also carries `{test}` tags for all five selector examples (`selector_nested`, `selector_impl_and_trait`, `selector_inline_and_foreign`, `selector_duplicate_names`, `selector_use`).

**Untested secondary cases**
- Duplicate impl blocks.
- Literal `%` escaping.
- Unnamed macro items.
- The test uses `contains` rather than an exact set.

The code for these cases is simple and follows the same tested paths.
